introduction-the-communication-gap.core: Software fails less from bad code than from misunderstanding the business. Domain-Driven Design puts the domain model at the centre: developers and domain experts collaborate on a shared language and model, split large domains into bounded contexts, and use tactical patterns (entities, value objects, aggregates, events, repositories) to express it in code.

first_principles.problem: Developers build 'customer' features that don't match what sales, billing and support each mean by customer.
truths: Words mean different things to different teams.

analogy.title: Translating a legal contract
analogy.story: Precise shared terms prevent costly misunderstandings between parties.
analogy.breaks: Contracts are fixed once signed; domain models keep evolving.

example.title: Event storming session
flow: Experts and devs place orange sticky notes for domain events

check.a: Building software around a rich model of the business domain, developed with domain experts.

ubiquitous-language-speaking-the-same-to.core: A ubiquitous language is a precise vocabulary shared by domain experts and developers within a bounded context, used in conversations, documentation and code (class, method and event names). When the language changes, the code changes. It eliminates translation errors between business and technical speak.

first_principles.problem: Business says 'policy lapse', code says 'subscription_status = 3', and bugs come from mistranslation.
derivation: Reject **technical jargon** in the domain layer.

analogy.title: A shared rulebook for a sport
analogy.story: Players, referees and commentators all mean the same thing by 'offside'.
analogy.breaks: Sports rules are fixed for a season; domain language evolves with the business.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Experts can read and validate the logic.

code.text:
# Before
if sub.status == 3: sub.flag = True
# After
if policy.premium_overdue_beyond_grace_period():
    policy.lapse(reason=LapseReason.NON_PAYMENT)

check.q: Why should domain terms appear directly in code?
check.a: It removes translation between business and technical language, reducing misunderstandings.

bounded-contexts-the-big-picture.core: A bounded context is an explicit boundary within which a particular model and language apply consistently. 'Customer' in Sales (leads, deals) differs from Billing (payment methods, invoices) and Support (tickets, SLAs). Each context owns its model and data, and context maps describe relationships between them (customer/supplier, conformist, anti-corruption layer, shared kernel). They often map well to microservices or modules.

first_principles.problem: A single 'Customer' class with 150 fields tries to serve every department and nobody can change it safely.
truths: One model can't serve every purpose.
derivation: Each context **owns its model and data**.

analogy.title: Different departments' views of the same person
analogy.story: HR sees an employee, payroll sees a salary record and IT sees an account.
analogy.breaks: Departments can walk down the hall; contexts integrate through explicit contracts.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each model stays small and focused.

check.a: A boundary within which a specific domain model and language are consistent.

tactical-ddd-entities-vs-value-objects.core: Entities have identity that persists through changes (a Customer with id 42 is the same customer after changing address). Value objects are defined only by their attributes and are immutable (Money(10, 'EUR'), Address, DateRange): two with the same values are equal. Prefer value objects to encode rules, validation and behaviour, keeping entities lean.

first_principles.problem: Money is a float passed everywhere, causing currency mix-ups and rounding bugs.
truths: Some things are tracked by identity.

analogy.title: A person versus a banknote
analogy.story: You're the same person after a haircut; any two €10 notes are interchangeable.
analogy.breaks: Banknotes have serial numbers; in the model, value objects truly have no identity.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Currency mistakes impossible to compile into the logic.

check.q: When are two value objects considered equal?
check.a: When all their attributes are equal.

aggregates-consistency-boundaries.core: An aggregate is a cluster of entities and value objects treated as one consistency unit, accessed only through its root (e.g. Order with its OrderLines). Invariants inside the aggregate are enforced transactionally; references to other aggregates are by ID only, and cross-aggregate consistency is eventual (via domain events). Keep aggregates small.

first_principles.problem: Order, Customer and Inventory are updated in one huge transaction, causing lock contention and deadlocks.
truths: Not everything must be immediately consistent.
derivation: Group them into an **aggregate with a root**.
Use **events** for cross-aggregate updates; keep aggregates **small**.

analogy.title: A sealed parcel with a packing list
analogy.story: Everything inside is checked together; other parcels are referenced by tracking number.
analogy.breaks: Parcels can be opened by anyone; aggregate internals must only change through the root.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Order invariants guaranteed; inventory updated via events.

check.q: How should one aggregate refer to another?
check.a: By identifier only, not by direct object reference.

domain-events-communicating-between-aggr.core: Domain events record that something meaningful happened in the domain (OrderPlaced, PaymentCaptured), named in the past tense in the ubiquitous language. Aggregates emit them; handlers in the same or other bounded contexts react, achieving eventual consistency without coupling. Publish them reliably with the transactional outbox pattern.

first_principles.problem: Placing an order must reserve stock and email the customer, but direct calls couple the Order aggregate to everything.
truths: Facts can be shared without dependencies.
Events must not be lost between DB write and publish.
derivation: Use the **outbox pattern** for reliable publishing.

analogy.title: Announcements on a company noticeboard
analogy.story: The sales team posts 'deal closed'; finance and delivery react on their own.
analogy.breaks: Noticeboards don't guarantee everyone reads them; the outbox and broker do.

example.title: Transactional outbox
flow: In one DB transaction: save Order + insert OrderPlaced into outbox table
Relay (Debezium/poller) publishes outbox rows to Kafka

check.q: What problem does the transactional outbox pattern solve?
check.a: Atomically saving state and recording an event, so events are never lost or published without the state change.

the-anti-corruption-layer-acl.core: An anti-corruption layer translates between your bounded context's model and an external or legacy system's model, so foreign concepts, naming and quirks don't leak into your domain. It typically combines adapters, translators and facades, isolating change when the other system evolves.

first_principles.problem: A new billing service adopts a legacy ERP's cryptic field names and status codes, and its model becomes as messy as the ERP.

analogy.title: An interpreter and cultural adviser at negotiations
analogy.story: Your team speaks its language; the interpreter handles the other side's idioms.
analogy.breaks: Interpreters can improvise; ACLs must explicitly handle every mapping.

example.title: Translating legacy status
example.outcome: a clean model despite messy neighbours.

check.q: What does an anti-corruption layer protect?
check.a: Your bounded context's model from foreign or legacy concepts leaking in.

repositories-abstracting-persistence.core: A repository provides a collection-like interface for loading and saving aggregates (orders.get(id), orders.save(order)), hiding storage details (SQL, ORM, document DB). One repository per aggregate root keeps persistence concerns out of the domain model and makes domain logic testable with in-memory implementations.

first_principles.problem: Domain logic is tangled with SQL queries, so it can't be tested without a database.
truths: Domain logic shouldn't depend on storage.
Aggregates are loaded and saved as units.

analogy.title: A library's checkout desk
analogy.story: You ask for a book by ID and return it there; you don't need to know the shelving system.
analogy.breaks: Libraries lend copies; repositories return the aggregate you must save back.

example.title: Repository interface and fake

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Domain tests run in milliseconds without a DB.

example.outcome: clean separation of domain and storage.

check.q: Why have one repository per aggregate root rather than per table?
check.a: Aggregates are the unit of consistency and persistence, so they're loaded and saved as wholes.
